text: Welcome to Chapter Two: Writing Data. Up to now you've only read data with SELECT. Starting here, you'll learn to add, change, and remove rows with INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE. This lesson covers the simplest case: inserting a single row with INSERT INTO and VALUES.

Because writing data can damage shared sample data, we'll practice on our own scratch table instead of a real AdventureWorks table. This CREATE TABLE statement builds dbo-dot-LessonDemo, with an auto-incrementing ProductID, a required ProductName and ListPrice, and an optional Color. This table is yours to insert into, update, and delete from throughout the whole chapter.

Here's the basic shape of an insert. INSERT INTO names the target table, followed by a parenthesized list of columns, then VALUES with a matching parenthesized list of literal values. ProductName lines up with Trail Bike, ListPrice with 799.99, and Color with Red. Values match columns by position, not by name.

T-SQL technically lets you skip the column list and supply values in the table's default order, but that's fragile. If someone adds a column later, or you misremember the order, the insert either fails or silently lands values in the wrong columns. Naming every column explicitly protects you from both problems.

Notice ProductID never appears in either list. It's declared IDENTITY(1,1), so SQL Server generates the next value automatically every time you insert. Right after the insert, SCOPE_IDENTITY returns the value it just assigned, which is handy when you need to reference the new row immediately.
Next, you'll insert several rows in one statement instead of repeating INSERT INTO one row at a time.
